issues.legal_issue: A mortgagee’s possession does not become possession as a family manager when the evidence establishes that it began under an independent mortgage.
material_facts: The defendant’s possession of the lands began under a usufructuary mortgage granted by the owner.
The appellant did not dispute the mortgage or contend that it had been taken on behalf of the family.
The mortgage was granted while the family manager was alive.
issues.conclusion: The contention that the defendant was precluded from acquiring title by adverse possession as a former family manager did not arise for decision, because his possession began as mortgagee and not as family manager.
issues.legal_principle: A claim that possession began in a representative or managerial capacity cannot govern where the possession is instead traced to an independent mortgage. The Court referred to Murugesam Pillai v. Manickavasaka Pandara and Guruswami Nadar v. Gopalaswami Odayar on the evidentiary effect of a party’s failure to testify, but found that question unnecessary to decide in light of the undisputed mortgage.

predicates.mortgage_possession_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a mortgagee’s possession can be treated as possession in a separate representative or managerial capacity.
predicates.possession_began_under_independent_mortg: The possessor first entered the property under a mortgage granted to that possessor.
predicates.mortgage_was_not_taken_for_family: The mortgage was not taken on behalf of the family whose title is later asserted.

issues.definition: When a dispute about the capacity in which possession began is resolved by an independent mortgage not taken for the family, a manager-based bar to adverse possession does not arise.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgagee’s possession may become adverse when the owner agrees to a change in the character of possession, even if the transaction effecting the change is legally inoperative.
material_facts: The defendant had entered possession as a usufructuary mortgagee.
An arrangement was alleged under which the earlier sale to the family member was cancelled and the owner then sold the lands to the mortgagee.
The cancellation endorsement was unregistered and could not transfer title back to the owner; the family therefore remained entitled to redeem the mortgage.
The Court held that the endorsement, considered together with the sale to the mortgagee, could be admitted to show the character of the mortgagee’s possession.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted that an agreement with the owner could change the character of a mortgagee’s possession and start adverse possession even if the transaction was inoperative in law. Whether that occurred depended on whether the family member was capable of consenting.
issues.legal_principle: A mortgagee cannot acquire title by unilateral declaration while continuing to possess as mortgagee, but may acquire title by prescription where an agreement with the owner changes the character of possession. The Court relied on Kanda Sami Pillai v. Chinnabba for that principle and Varatha Pillai v. Jeevanathammal for admitting the cancellation endorsement with the subsequent sale as evidence of the character of possession. The ineffective cancellation did not itself transfer title, so the owner’s successor remained entitled to redeem absent adverse possession.

predicates.mortgage_redemption_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claimant’s right to redeem property held by a mortgagee.
predicates.possession_began_as_mortgagee: The possessor entered the property in the capacity of a mortgagee.
predicates.owner_agreed_to_change_possession_capaci: The owner agreed that the possessor would hold the property in a capacity different from that of mortgagee.
predicates.change_was_evidenced_by_an_inoperative_t: The asserted change in capacity was evidenced by a transaction that could not effect the intended legal transfer.

issues.definition: A mortgagee’s possession may become adverse where possession began under a mortgage and the owner agreed to change its character, even if the transaction evidencing that change was legally inoperative.

issues.legal_issue: A person who was a minor cannot consent to an arrangement that changes possession lawful at its inception into adverse possession.
material_facts: The proposed change in the mortgagee’s possession depended on an arrangement involving the family member who had acquired the earlier sale deed.
The appellant contended that this family member was a minor when the arrangement was made.
The evidence and issues below did not determine whether the family member was then a minor or an adult.
issues.conclusion: If the family member was a minor when the arrangement was made, it could not change the character of the mortgagee’s possession, because a minor cannot give the consent required for that change. The Court remanded the matter to determine the family member’s age at that time.
issues.legal_principle: Possession lawful at its inception can change into adverse possession through an agreement with the owner, but not through an arrangement requiring the consent of a minor, who is legally incapable of giving consent. The Court accepted that adverse possession may arise against a minor in some circumstances, referring to Sitharama Raju v. Subba Raju, but distinguished the specific question of changing possession lawful at inception by the minor’s consent.

rule.if: mortgage_redemption_dispute and possession_was_lawful_at_inception and change_depended_on_owner_consent and owner_was_a_minor

predicates.mortgage_redemption_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claimant’s right to redeem property held by a mortgagee.
predicates.possession_was_lawful_at_inception: The possessor originally entered the property lawfully as a mortgagee.
predicates.change_depended_on_owner_consent: The asserted change in the character of possession depended on the owner agreeing to it.
predicates.owner_was_a_minor: The owner whose agreement was required was legally a minor when the arrangement was made.

issues.definition: Where possession began lawfully and its change into adverse possession depended on the owner’s consent, the arrangement cannot change its character if that owner was a minor.

issues.legal_issue: A possession suit asserting a right that is properly a right to redeem may, in the interests of resolving long-pending litigation, be treated as a redemption suit and remanded for amendment.
material_facts: The appellant brought a suit for possession, but the rights asserted on the basis of the earlier sale deed gave the appellant a right to redeem the usufructuary mortgage.
The suit was not framed as one for redemption.
The litigation had been pending for a long time, and the Court considered it desirable to determine the parties’ rights without requiring a separate action.
issues.conclusion: Although the suit as framed was for possession rather than redemption, the Court treated it as a redemption suit, directed an amendment of the plaint, and remanded the matter for a fresh inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: A suit seeking ejectment may be dismissed when the claimant’s right is to redeem a mortgage rather than to obtain immediate possession. However, where litigation has long been pending, the Court may decide the parties’ rights on the footing that the suit is for redemption and direct the pleadings to be amended.

predicates.property_possession_suit: The claimant filed a suit seeking possession of property held by another.
predicates.claimant_entitlement_is_redemption: The claimant’s asserted right is to redeem a mortgage rather than to obtain possession without redemption.
predicates.litigation_has_long_been_pending: The proceedings have been pending for a prolonged period.

issues.definition: When a long-pending possession suit asserts a right to redeem, the court may treat it as a redemption suit and remand it for amendment.
